title: Review: Series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws; Resistivity; Potential dividers; EMF and internal resistance
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL04-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL08-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL08-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL04-uk1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL06-1#N.11, EL04-1#N.4, EL04-uk1#N.10, EL06-1#N.7, EL06-uk1#N.3, EL07-1#N.12, EL08-1#N.3, EL04-1#N.10a, EL04-uk1#N.3, EL06-1#N.2, EL06-uk1#N.9, EL07-1#N.8. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Resistance
items.clue: Quantity proportional to the length of a wire and to 1/A.

items.label: emf
items.clue: Energy transferred to each coulomb of charge by the source.

items.label: Short circuit
items.clue: Connection with R = 0, giving a very large current that heats the cell.

items.label: Voltmeter
items.clue: Instrument connected across the chosen length of wire, giving V for R = V/I.

questions.stem: Three identical lamps are connected to a supply of negligible internal resistance: lamp A is in series with lamps B and C, which are in parallel with each other. The filament of lamp C breaks. What happens to the brightness of lamps A and B? (Assume each lamp's resistance stays the same.)

options.text: A and B both go out, because the circuit is now broken.
A becomes dimmer and B becomes brighter.
A stays the same and B becomes brighter, because B now carries C's current.
A becomes brighter and B stays the same, because the parallel branch keeps its potential difference.

questions.stem: A uniform copper wire is cut into two pieces of equal length. How do the resistance and the resistivity of one piece compare with those of the original wire?

options.text: Its resistance and its resistivity are both halved.
Its resistance and its resistivity are both the same.
Its resistance is the same, but its resistivity is halved.
Its resistance is halved; its resistivity is unchanged.

questions.stem: A cable is made from a ceramic superconductor with a critical temperature of 92 K. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It needs liquid helium (4 K), since every superconductor must be close to absolute zero.
Liquid nitrogen (77 K) keeps it superconducting, so it can carry a current with no heating.
It superconducts at room temperature, since 92 is well above zero.
At 77 K its resistivity is very small but not zero, so it still heats slightly.

questions.explanation: Right. 77 K is below 92 K, so its resistivity is zero: no energy is transferred as heat, however large the current.

questions.stem: Resistors of 3.0 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 8.0 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?
Three cells are connected in series in a single line: two of emf 1.5 V face one way, and one of emf 2.0 V faces the other way. What is the total emf of the line?
questions.explanation: Right. 1.5 + 1.5 − 2.0 = 1.0 V, in the direction the two 1.5 V cells push.

questions.stem: An NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor are in series across a supply of constant pd. An ideal voltmeter is connected across the thermistor. The thermistor is warmed. What happens to the voltmeter reading?

options.text: It increases, because warming releases more charge carriers in the thermistor.
It stays the same, because the series current is the same in both components.
It decreases: the thermistor's resistance falls, so its share of the pd falls.
It increases, because heating raises its resistance, as it does in a metal wire.

questions.explanation: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as it warms. It becomes a smaller fraction of the total resistance, so the pd across it falls.

questions.stem: A battery with an internal resistance of 0.50 Ω drives a current of 0.60 A through a lamp, and an ideal voltmeter across the battery's terminals reads 4.2 V. The lamp is then disconnected, so that only the voltmeter remains connected across the battery. What does the voltmeter now read?
questions.explanation: emf = terminal potential difference + Ir = 4.2 + 0.60 × 0.50 = 4.5 V. With no current, the voltmeter reads the emf.

questions.stem: Wire X has resistance R and is made of a material of resistivity ρ. Wire Y is made of the same material at the same temperature, but it is half as long as X and has half the diameter of X. What are the resistance and the resistivity of wire Y?
questions.explanation: R ∝ length ÷ area: the length factor is ½ and the area factor is ¼, so R_Y = (½ ÷ ¼)R = 2R. Same material and temperature, so the same ρ.

questions.stem: A student plots R against length for a uniform wire of diameter 0.40 mm. The best-fit line has a gradient of 4.0 Ω m⁻¹ and crosses the R axis at 0.30 Ω. What is the resistivity of the wire?
questions.explanation: A = π(0.40 × 10⁻³)²/4 = 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ m². ρ = gradient × A = 4.0 × 1.26 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. The 0.30 Ω intercept (contact resistance) does not affect the gradient.

questions.stem: Three circuits are each made from an identical cell of negligible internal resistance, a resistor and a lamp. In circuit 1 the three form a single closed loop. Circuit 2 is the same loop with an open switch added. Circuit 3 is the same loop as circuit 1 with a wire of negligible resistance connected directly across the lamp's terminals. Which ranks the currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ in the lamps of circuits 1, 2 and 3?

A 15 V supply charges a 12 V battery. They are connected in a single loop, positive terminal to positive terminal, and the total resistance in the loop is 2.0 Ω. What is the current, and which way does it pass through the battery?

options.text: 13.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal
7.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal

questions.explanation: Right. Net emf = 15 − 12 = 3.0 V, so I = 1.5 A. The larger emf wins and drives current backwards through the battery: that is charging.

questions.stem: An LDR and a 10 kΩ fixed resistor are in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected across the fixed resistor. The LDR's resistance is 50 kΩ in the dark and 1.0 kΩ in bright light. What does the voltmeter read in each case?

options.text: 5.0 V in the dark; 0.55 V in bright light
5.5 V in the dark; 1.0 V in bright light
1.0 V in the dark; 5.5 V in bright light

questions.explanation: Dark: 6.0 × 10/(10 + 50) = 1.0 V. Bright: 6.0 × 10/(10 + 1.0) = 5.5 V. The fixed resistor's share rises as the LDR's resistance falls.
